title: Using OSS models to build AI apps with millions of users — Hassan El Mghari

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 69%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on product design and UX decisions for AI apps, with 80% of build time on UI and mobile-first design as core principles. The demonstrated apps span consumer productivity tools, creative image generation, and general utilities without a single vertical focus. Hassan covers the full lifecycle from maintaining an idea shortlist through building, launching, and iterating on AI products. Prerequisites include full-stack development familiarity and TypeScript/Next.js comfort, targeting intermediate builders. Recorded conference talk at AI Engineer World's Fair combining live demos, architecture walkthrough, and practical tips. All supporting evidence is directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Hassan El Mghari, who leads developer relations at Together AI, presents his approach to building open source AI applications that collectively reach millions of users. Together AI provides inference APIs for open source models across modalities, including chat (Qwen 3), reasoning (DeepSeek R1), image (Flux), vision, and audio, plus dedicated instances, fine-tuning, and GPU clusters. He argues it is an historic time to build because AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt, Vzero, and Lovable have lowered the barrier to entry while groundbreaking models arrive weekly. He demos several apps: a glasses-picker, a git commit-message writer with 40,000 installs, a text-to-app builder with ~1M users and 5M requests, an image generation app with 1M+ users and 48M images generated, Napkins (screenshot-to-app, 40k users), a resume-to-personal-site builder, a menu visualizer, an AI tutor, and OCR tools. His core architecture is intentionally minimal: user input, one API call to an AI model on Together AI, optional database storage, and display to the user. His tech stack is Next.js and TypeScript, Together AI for models, Neon for serverless Postgres, Clerk for auth, Prisma as ORM, Shadcn and Tailwind for styling, S3 for image uploads, Plausible for analytics, Helicone for LLM analytics, and Vercel for hosting. He notes most users access his apps on mobile, making mobile UX critical. His seven-step build process covers keeping a running idea list with a top-five short list, choosing a short memorable name, designing the screens, building the simplest possible working version targeting one API endpoint, adding auth and rate limits as needed, prepping for launch with OG image, domain, analytics, and a clean README, then launching via LinkedIn or X. He then offers seven tips: think of a simple idea describable in five words, spend 80% of time on UI, keep to one or two API calls, incorporate the latest models (e.g., launching Blinkshot with Flux Chanel two days after release), launch early and iterate, make apps free and open source, and keep shipping because it is a numbers game. In Q&A he explains he keeps apps free and open source because he enjoys teaching and gets company sponsorships for compute; he advises builders to request credits from infrastructure companies. He notes apps with built-in viral sharing loops perform best, and that swapping in newer AI models is often a one-line change that can unlock improvements.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Keep a running idea list and maintain a top-five short list so you are ready to build when inspiration or a new model arrives.
Aim for radical simplicity: a single AI API call from user input to displayed result enables fast iteration and idea validation.
Spend roughly 80% of time on UI; good design drives adoption even for ideas as simple as PDF summarization.
Most users access AI apps on mobile, so mobile UX is critical from the start.
Incorporate the latest AI models quickly; launching shortly after a new model release increases virality potential.
Launch early and iterate; even after 40 apps Hassan still cannot predict what will succeed, so minimizing build time de-risks each attempt.
Build in viral sharing loops with nice OG images so users can easily share what they create.
Open-sourcing everything maximizes reach, community contributions, and discoverability, and makes infrastructure companies willing to sponsor compute.
Reach out to AI infra companies for credits; they often sponsor open source projects.
It is a numbers game: keep shipping because volume and repetition improve idea selection and build speed.

sections.title: Introduction and Together AI Overview
sections.summary: Hassan introduces himself as leader of developer relations at Together AI, a platform providing inference APIs for open source models across chat, reasoning, image, vision, and audio modalities, plus dedicated instances, fine-tuning, and GPU clusters. He has averaged roughly one AI app per month for four years, all open source.

sections.title: Why It Is a Historic Time to Build
sections.summary: Hassan argues the barrier to building has lowered dramatically thanks to AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt, Vzero, and Lovable, while groundbreaking models arrive weekly, making it an exceptional time to create AI applications.

sections.title: App Demos
sections.summary: Hassan briefly demos multiple apps: a glasses picker from a Twitter request, a commit-message writer with 40k installs, a text-to-app builder with ~1M users and 5M requests, an image generation app with 1M+ users and 48M images, Napkins (screenshot-to-app) with 40k users, a resume-to-personal-site builder, a menu visualizer, an AI tutor, and OCR tools.

sections.title: Architecture and Tech Stack
sections.summary: Hassan describes his intentionally simple architecture: user input, one AI model API call on Together AI, optional database storage, and display to the user. His stack is Next.js/TypeScript, Together AI, Neon serverless Postgres, Clerk auth, Prisma ORM, Shadcn/Tailwind styling, S3 for images, Plausible analytics, Helicone for LLM analytics, and Vercel hosting. He notes most users are on mobile.

sections.title: Build Process from Idea to Launch
sections.summary: Hassan outlines seven steps: keep a running idea list with a top-five short list, pick a short memorable name, design the screens, build the simplest possible working version targeting one API endpoint, add auth and rate limits, prep for launch with OG image, domain, analytics, and a clean README, then launch via LinkedIn or X.

sections.title: Seven Tips for Building Apps and Q&A
sections.summary: Hassan shares seven tips: pick a simple idea describable in five words, spend 80% of time on UI, keep to one or two API calls, incorporate the latest AI models (e.g., launching Blinkshot two days after Flux Chanel), launch early and iterate, make apps free and open source, and keep shipping as a numbers game. In Q&A he explains he keeps apps free because he enjoys teaching and gets company sponsorships for compute from Together AI, Neon, and Clerk; advises builders to request credits from infra companies; notes apps with viral sharing loops perform best; and says swapping in newer AI models is often a one-line change.
